title: Speaking Up (Whistleblowing)
blurb: What whistleblowing is, what to speak up about, who to tell, and how you are protected.
siteNotes: Who the business owners are and how to contact them if a concern involves a manager or the General Manager
Where the grievance procedure is kept
legalNotes: Protection for workers who make a protected disclosure: Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 (Employment Rights Act 1996, Part IVA). The trainer does not cite it.

CHECK: the trainer says the law protects people who raise concerns "in good faith". Since 2013 the legal test is a reasonable belief that the disclosure is in the public interest, not good faith (good faith can only affect compensation). Wording kept as the trainer has it; confirm whether to change.
CHECK: the trainer says concerns go to the manager or General Manager, then the business owners. Confirm the venue's whistleblowing policy names the same route.

cards.title: Speaking Up (Whistleblowing)
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- say what whistleblowing is and what to speak up about
- tell it apart from a personal grievance
- know who to tell and that you are protected

cards.title: Raising a genuine concern
cards.body:
Sometimes you might become aware of something seriously wrong at work. Speaking up about it is one of the most important things you can do.

Whistleblowing is raising a genuine concern about wrongdoing, and the law specifically protects people who do it in good faith.

cards.title: Serious wrongdoing
cards.body: Things worth speaking up about include:

items.title: Danger
items.text: To health, safety or food safety

items.title: Harm or risk
items.text: To a guest, child or vulnerable adult

cards.title: Whistleblowing or grievance?
cards.body: It is different from a personal complaint about your own job, which should go through the grievance procedure.

left.title: Speak up
items: A serious breach of the law

right.title: Grievance procedure
items: A personal complaint about your own job

cards.title: Start with your manager
cards.body:
You should normally raise a concern with your manager or the General Manager.

If that is not appropriate, for example because it involves them, raise it with the business owners.

You do not need cast-iron proof. You just need to genuinely believe something is wrong.

items.title: Your manager or the General Manager

cards.title: Taken seriously, never victimised
cards.body:
Concerns raised in good faith are taken seriously and handled as confidentially as possible. Nobody will be victimised or treated badly for speaking up.

> Staying silent can let real harm continue. If something is not right, please say something.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Whistleblowing is raising a genuine concern about wrongdoing
- The law protects people who do it in good faith
- Tell your manager or the General Manager, or the owners if it involves them
- You do not need cast-iron proof
- Nobody will be victimised; staying silent lets harm continue

options: Raising a genuine concern about wrongdoing at work
Complaining about your own rota or pay
Reporting a guest who was rude to you
Reminding a colleague about the rules
cards.why: Whistleblowing is raising a genuine concern about wrongdoing at work.

cards.q: The law protects people who whistleblow in good faith.
cards.why: The law specifically protects people who raise a genuine concern in good faith.

cards.q: Who should you normally raise a concern with first?
options: A guest who saw it too
A friend outside the business
Your manager or the General Manager
The supplier involved
cards.why: You should normally raise a concern with your manager or the General Manager.

cards.q: You need cast-iron proof before you can raise a concern.
cards.why: You do not need cast-iron proof; you just need to genuinely believe something is wrong.

cards.q: Which of these is a kind of wrongdoing worth speaking up about?
options: A danger to health, safety or food safety
A dislike of a new uniform
A disagreement about holiday dates
A slow day in the restaurant
cards.why: Speak up about theft or fraud, danger to health, safety or food safety, harm to a guest, child or vulnerable adult, serious breaches of the law, and cover-ups.

cards.q: Whistleblowing is the same as a personal grievance about your own job.
cards.why: A personal complaint about your own job goes through the grievance procedure.

cards.q: If a concern involves your manager, you can raise it with:
options: No one, as it is awkward
The business owners
A guest
Another team's supervisor only
cards.why: If it is not appropriate to go to your manager, you can raise it with the business owners.

cards.q: People who raise a genuine concern will be victimised.
cards.why: Nobody will be victimised or treated badly for speaking up.

cards.q: Concerns are handled as confidentially as possible.
cards.why: Concerns raised in good faith are taken seriously and handled as confidentially as possible.

cards.q: Staying silent about serious wrongdoing can:
options: Let harm continue
Make the problem go away
Protect the guest
Show loyalty to the team
cards.why: Staying silent can let real harm continue.
